t: Number of Adjacent Elements With the Same Color — Incremental Counter Maintenance
o: Instead of rescanning the array after each paint (O(nq) = 1e10 worst case), maintain a running count of equal adjacent pairs. Painting index i only affects the pairs (i−1,i) and (i,i+1): subtract contributions of old color, apply the new color, add new contributions. Uncolored cells (0) never match since colors are ≥ 1. Example 1 walks through exactly these local updates, ending at count 2. O(1) per query.
k: Only the two neighboring pairs of the painted index change — update the global count locally.
Color 0 means uncolored and never equals a real color (colors ≥ 1), so uncolored neighbors contribute nothing.

a.i: Before repainting, decrement the count for each existing matching neighbor pair of the old color; after repainting, increment for matches with the new color. Append the running count per query.
s: Keep colors array initialized to 0 and counter c = 0.
Per query: remove old-color adjacencies at i−1,i and i,i+1 if old color ≠ 0.
Set the new color; add adjacencies matching it.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def colorTheArray(self, n: int, queries: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        col = [0] * n
        c = 0
        ans = []
        for i, x in queries:
            if col[i] != 0:
                if i > 0 and col[i - 1] == col[i]: c -= 1
                if i < n - 1 and col[i + 1] == col[i]: c -= 1
            col[i] = x
            if i > 0 and col[i - 1] == x: c += 1
            if i < n - 1 and col[i + 1] == x: c += 1
            ans.append(c)
        return ans

a.t: O(n + q) — array init plus O(1) per query

w: The delta-update pattern generalizes to any 'count property under point updates' problem. Pitfalls: repainting with the same color (old removals and new additions cancel correctly — verify), and boundary indices 0 and n−1. Follow-up: range paints (need a segment tree storing per-segment left/right colors and internal match counts).
